title: Ensemble Learning
oneLiner: Many imperfect models, combined well, beat one carefully chosen model: bagging, random forests, AdaBoost and gradient boosting.

what.html:
Ensemble learning trains several models (base learners) and combines their predictions into one. If the members are reasonably good and make different mistakes, the combined vote is more accurate and more stable than any single member.

Everyday versionAsking one doctor might get you a wrong diagnosis; asking a panel of independent doctors and going with the majority is much safer, as long as each doctor is better than guessing and they didn't all learn from the same mistaken textbook.

Two families: bagging (train members in parallel on random resamples and vote; random forests add random features) and boosting (train members one after another, each fixing the previous ones' mistakes: AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost).

why.html:
• Accuracy. Random forests and gradient-boosted trees are the go-to models for tabular data and win many competitions.
  • Stability. Averaging reduces the variance of unstable learners like deep trees.
  • Weak to strong. Boosting turns learners barely better than guessing into a strong classifier.
  • Bonus outputs: feature importances, out-of-bag error estimates, and natural parallelism (bagging).

how.title: One model or many?
how.html: Occam's razor says pick the simplest model that explains the data. The No Free Lunch theorem says no algorithm is always best: each makes assumptions and fails in different places. So instead of searching for one perfect expert, build a committee.

how.title: Members must be diverse
how.html: A committee of clones adds nothing. Diversity comes from different algorithms, different hyperparameters, different input representations (audio + video, image + text) or different training sets (random samples, or regions of the input space: a "mixture of experts").

how.title: Combining their answers
how.html: Simple rules: average (or weighted average) the predicted probabilities, take the median, min, max or product, or let each member vote. In the session's table, every rule picks class C₂.

how.title: When does an ensemble help?
how.html: Two conditions: members are better than random (error below 0.5 for two classes) and their errors are independent. Then 25 members each wrong 35% of the time give a majority vote that is wrong only 6% of the time. If members are worse than random, voting makes it worse.

how.title: Bagging: bootstrap and vote
how.html: Draw M bootstrap samples (same size, drawn with replacement), train one model on each, then average (regression) or vote (classification). In the session's example, ten one-split trees each get at most 7 of 10 points right, yet their vote gets all 10.

how.title: What bagging can and can't fix
how.html: Bagging mainly reduces variance, so it shines with unstable learners (deep trees). For a stable, biased learner it barely helps, and each bootstrap sample only contains about 63% of the distinct records (37% are left out), which can even hurt.

how.title: Random forests: bagging + random features
how.html: Grow many unpruned trees on bootstrap samples, and at every split let the tree look at only a random subset of features. That stops every tree from using the same strong feature at the top, so the trees are less correlated and their vote is better.

how.title: Forests also rank features
how.html: Random forests handle thousands of variables, work for classification and regression, and report how much each feature reduced impurity. On the iris flowers, petal length (0.44) and petal width (0.42) matter far more than the sepal measurements.

how.title: Boosting: learn from mistakes, in sequence
how.html: Train a model, look at which points it got wrong, give those points more weight, and train the next model to focus on them. The final model is a weighted vote of all the members.

how.title: AdaBoost's two formulas
how.html: Each member's say is α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε): low error ε gives a big α. Then misclassified points are multiplied by eα, correct ones by e−α, and the weights are renormalised. The ensemble predicts sign(Σ α·h(x)).

how.title: AdaBoost on the example
how.html: Three stumps with α = 1.738, 2.778, 4.119. For x = 0.65 they say −1, +1, −1. The weighted votes are 2.778 for +1 and 1.738 + 4.119 = 5.857 for −1, so the answer is −1.

how.title: Gradient boosting: fit the residuals
how.html: Start with a constant prediction (the mean). Compute the residuals y − F(x), the part the model still gets wrong, and fit a small tree to them. Add a fraction (learning rate) of that tree to the model. Repeat. Residuals are the negative gradient of squared loss, hence the name.

how.title: Gradient boosting by hand
how.html: Weights 88, 76, 56, 73, 77, 57: F₀ = 71.2. The first tree predicts the residuals (e.g. +16.8 for the first person), and with learning rate 0.1 their prediction becomes 71.2 + 1.68 = 72.9; after the second tree, 74.4. Small steps, steadily closer to 88.

how.title: XGBoost
how.html: An optimised, distributed gradient-boosting library: regularisation against overfitting, tree pruning, built-in handling of missing values, parallel tree building, cache-aware and out-of-core computing, and built-in cross-validation.

demo.html: Start with 1 tree of depth 12: it fits the training points almost perfectly but its boundary is jagged, and test accuracy suffers. Slide the number of trees up to 60: the forest's boundary smooths out and test accuracy rises. Then untick bootstrap and random features: all trees become identical and the forest is no better than one tree. Diversity is the whole trick.

example.html:
Mixture of experts and multimodal inputs. The examples of diversity: spoken words plus video of the speaker, or images plus text annotations, each handled by a different member.

Predicting weight from height, age and gender with gradient boosting (worked in full).

Supplementary Mobile operators use gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) to predict customer churn and cell congestion from hundreds of tabular KPIs; random forests are a common baseline for fault classification.

misunderstandings: Only if they are diverse and better than random; correlated members add little.
Bagging mainly reduces variance; boosting reduces bias (and variance) by focusing on errors.
With too many rounds, deep trees or a high learning rate it can; use a small learning rate, shallow trees and early stopping.
Random forests use a random subset of features per tree.
The classic algorithm resamples features at every split, not once per tree.
takeaways: Ensembles combine diverse base learners; they beat single models when members are better than random and their errors are independent.
Combine by voting or averaging (sum, weighted sum, median, min, max, product).
Bagging trains on bootstrap samples in parallel and votes; it reduces variance.
Random forests = bagged unpruned trees + random features at each split; they also give feature importances.
Boosting trains sequentially: AdaBoost reweights mistakes (α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε)); gradient boosting fits residuals (negative gradients) with a learning rate.
thirty: Ensemble learning combines several base learners, by voting or averaging, so that their different mistakes cancel out. It works when members are better than random and their errors are reasonably independent. Bagging trains each model on a bootstrap sample and votes, which mostly reduces variance. Random forests bag unpruned decision trees and pick a random subset of features at every split, which decorrelates the trees. Boosting builds models one after another: AdaBoost increases the weight of misclassified points and gives each model a say α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε), while gradient boosting fits each new tree to the residuals of the current model and adds it with a small learning rate.
